Remap severity values to the schema union 'deadly' | 'toxic' | 'unpalatable': water hemlock and poison hemlock stay `deadly`; Ipomoea pandurata (purgative, causes vomiting) becomes `toxic`; the perennial-sunflowers group and groundnut become `unpalatable`. Remove the invented values `unpleasant` and `harmless`.

Close the water-hemlock chambering inversion. State explicitly that the chambering is in the ROOTSTOCK/CROWN only and that Cicuta's individual fleshy finger roots are solid — so 'solid flesh, no chambers' can never be used as confirmation that a dug root is sunchoke. Only a tuber physically traced along an intact rhizome to a marked sunchoke stalk counts. Currently the entry presents the lengthwise cut as 'the decisive tell on the part you are actually harvesting,' which is precisely the part where it fails.

Add pokeweed (Phytolacca americana) as a lookalike with danger `toxic`: same disturbed/edge/moist habitat, thick dead stalks standing through the winter dig season, large fleshy taproot that is the most toxic part of the plant and a documented cause of adult poisoning when dug and mistaken for an edible root. Tell: one large vertical taproot from a single crown, never a chain of knobs at the end of a horizontal rhizome.
reasons: BLOCKER (safety-critical serialization bug): the entry uses `severity` on every lookalike, but the Lookalike interface in /Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/src/data/foraging.ts defines the key as `danger`. /Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/src/components/ForageSection.tsx:69 computes `const deadly = s.lookalikes.filter((l) => l.danger === 'deadly')` — with `severity` keys every `l.danger` is undefined, so the deadly-lookalike warning for water hemlock NEVER RENDERS, and the per-lookalike badge at line 110 (`{l.danger}`) prints blank next to 'Water hemlock'. This entry's entire justification is that a deadly confusable exists; publishing it as-is ships it with that signal switched off.

BLOCKER: two of the three severity values are not in the schema union `'deadly' | 'toxic' | 'unpalatable'`. The entry uses `unpleasant` (Ipomoea pandurata) and `harmless` (twice). `harmless` has no equivalent in the union at all — the closest legitimate value is `unpalatable`. Ipomoea pandurata, described in the entry's own text as a strong purgative that will make you vomit, should map to `toxic`, not to a softer invented label.

BLOCKER: invalid and incomplete region IDs. Valid RegionIds (/Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/src/data/seasonal-regional.ts) are northeast, southeast, midwest, southcentral, mountain, west. The entry declares `southwest` and `northwest`, which do not exist and match nothing in `forageFor()`'s exact-match filter, while OMITTING `southcentral` (TX, OK) — despite the habitat text explicitly describing south Texas and the Gulf Coast as core season-extending range. Result: the entry is invisible to South Central users and carries two dead tags.

BLOCKER (a stated tell that inverts fatally on the part being harvested): the entry's 'decisive tell' is to cut the crown lengthwise and read chambering, concluding 'A sunchoke tuber is solid all the way through - no chambers.' The entry's own cited source (Texas A&M Rangeplants) places the chambers in the ROOTSTOCK — 'short rootstocks have air cavities or chambers separated by cross-partitions' — while the plant bears separate 'fleshy or fleshy-tuberous roots' off that base. Cicuta's individual finger roots are SOLID. A forager who lifts a cluster of detached Cicuta finger roots, cuts one, and finds solid white flesh gets a false positive from the entry's own decisive test. The entry gestures at this ('hard to read on a small crown or on a crown snapped off and left in the ground') but never states the fact that closes the loop.

Missing toxic lookalike: pokeweed (Phytolacca americana). It occupies exactly the terrain this entry sends people to (disturbed ground, edges, moist old fields, fencerows), its thick dead stalks stand through the winter dig season alongside sunchoke stalks, and it stores a large fleshy taproot that is the most toxic part of the plant. Documented adult poisonings come specifically from digging the root and mistaking it for an edible one. Easy to distinguish (single large taproot, not knobs on a rhizome) — which is exactly why the tell should be written down rather than left out.

Region overreach on `west`: in this schema `west` = CA, OR, WA, HI, AK. The entry's own habitat text states the species is absent from Hawaii and Alaska. Tagging `west` surfaces a dig-in-wet-ditches entry to HI/AK users where the target plant does not occur but Cicuta does.

Verification note (not blocking): the CDC MMWR URL returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch, so I could not independently confirm the quoted 'artichokes, celery, sweet potatoes, sweet anise, or wild parsnip' wording or the three-bites detail. The quote matches the well-known 1992 Maine report and the citation is very likely sound; flagging only because it is the single load-bearing source for the `expert` rating.

What holds up, for the record: months are CORRECT — the schema comments `0 = January`, so [9,10,11,0,1,2,3] is Oct-Apr and matches the prose windows exactly. Scientific name Helianthus tuberosus is correct and unambiguous. Caution `expert` is the maximum level and is warranted, not too low. Both deadly lookalikes that actually matter (Cicuta spp. incl. C. douglasii regional replacement, and Conium maculatum) are present, and the seasonal-failure analysis for each — purple blotching weathering off dead stalks, first-year rosettes never having it, umbel skeletons persisting into the dig season — is better than most published treatments. The mark-in-flower-then-trace-the-rhizome protocol and the 'finding a tuber is NOT proof' anti-inversion paragraph are genuinely good. The inulin preparation guidance is complete and no leaching/detox step is missing.

Verdict: the botany is strong but the entry is not publishable in its current form. The `severity`/`danger` mismatch alone is disqualifying because it disables the exact warning this entry exists to deliver, and the Cicuta chambering inversion is a wording defect on the one test a forager applies to the thing in their hand.
